132	**The arithmetic steps are exact bit-by-bit identities on 32-bit registers**, not approximations: for example `nand(x,y) + x + 1` equals `x and not y` for every pair of 32-bit numbers (not (x and y) is minus one minus (x and y); adding x and one leaves x minus (x and y), which has no borrow), and `(not x or y) - y` equals `not x and not y` (the bits of y are a subset of those of (not x or y)). 133	
134	**Sharing.** What the programs of one task share is the circuit far more than the instruction string: the top NOT circuit is run by 13,520 Avida programs in 7,925 distinct sequences through 347 distinct route strings; the top NAND circuit by 17,037 programs in 8,942 sequences through 147. The most common circuits of AND, OR, NOR, XOR and EQU are each confined to one to seven runs: each run's program ancestry settled on its own circuits. Grouped by the set of bit-by-bit functions their parts compute (whatever instructions compute them), the reduced circuits fall into 16 (XOR) to 283 (OR) groups.
135	
136	### 3.1 One worked example per task, in the instruction set's terms and in plain logic
137	
138	A, B, C are Avida's fixed inputs `0x0f13149f`, `0x3308e53e`, `0x556241eb`; AX, BX, CX the three registers; each line is one executed instruction from Avida's trace, with its site (position in the instruction sequence). The worked program is the most common sequence of the task's most common reduced circuit; its required instructions are listed in the `.json` (`worked_examples`).
139	
140	- **NOT** (low seed 2, 44 programs): 11 `IO` reads B into BX; 12 `push`; 16 `pop`+`nop-C` puts B into CX; 20 `nand`: BX := nand(B, B) = `0xccf71ac1`; 21 `swap` to CX; 26 `IO`+`nop-C` writes it. Plain logic: **not B**.
141	- **NAND** (the same sequence): B brought into BX (11, 12, 16, 21); 34 `IO`+`nop-C` reads A into CX; 49 `nand`: BX := nand(B, A) = `0xfcfffbe1`; 51 `swap`; 56 `IO`+`nop-C` writes it. Plain logic: **not (A and B)**.
142	- **AND** (low seed 1, 27 programs): 39 `IO` reads C into BX; 40 `IO`+`nop-C` reads A into CX; 42 `nand`: nand(C, A) = `0xfafdff74`; 43 `nand`: nand(that, A) = `0xf5eeebeb` (not A or C); 45 `add` A: `0x0502008a`; 47 `inc`: `0x0502008b`; 53 `IO` writes it. Plain logic: **A and C** (`0x0f13149f and 0x556241eb = 0x0502008b`).
143	- **ORN** (low seed 2, 44 programs): B into BX (11, 12, 16, 21); 26 `IO`+`nop-C` reads C into CX; 28 `nand`+`nop-C`: CX := nand(B, C) = `0xeeffbed5`; 30 `nand`+`nop-C`: CX := nand(B, that) = `0xddf75beb`; 34 `IO`+`nop-C` writes it. Plain logic: **C or not B**.
144	- **OR** (default seed 1, 12 programs): 33 `IO`+`nop-C` reads A into CX; 41 and 45 `IO` (outside the route: rotation); 47 `IO` reads A into BX; 48 `IO`+`nop-A` reads B into AX; 52 `nand`: BX := nand(A, A) = not A; 61 `swap`+`nop-C` brings B into CX; 63 `nand`+`nop-C`: CX := nand(not A, B) = A or not B; 65 `nand`+`nop-A`: AX := nand(not A, A or not B) = `0x3f1bf5bf`; 69 and 73 `swap`; 78 `IO`+`nop-A` writes AX. Plain logic: **A or B**.
145	- **ANDN** (low seed 3, 28 programs): 47 `IO`+`nop-C` reads A into CX; 53 `IO` reads C into BX; 57 `nand`: nand(C, A); 60 `add`+`nop-C`: CX := that + A; 63 `inc`+`nop-C`: `0x0a111414`; 66 `IO`+`nop-C` writes it. Plain logic: **A and not C**.
146	- **NOR** (low seed 3, 28 programs): A and C read (47, 53); 57 `nand`, 60 `add`, 63 `inc`, 65 `sub`: BX := nand(C, A) − (A and not C) = `0xf0eceb60` = not A; 66 `IO`+`nop-C` reads B; 75 `nand`: A or not B; 78 `nand`: A or B = `0x3f1bf5bf`; 81 `push`, 83 `pop`; 85 `nand`: nand(A or B, A or B) = `0xc0e40a40`; 89 `IO` writes it. Plain logic: **not (A or B)**; C enters and cancels.
147	- **XOR** (default seed 1, 12 programs): 43 `nand`: nand(B, A) (pushed at 44); not A (52), A or not B (63), A or B (65) as for OR; 71 `pop`; 72 `nand`: nand(not (A and B), A or B) = A equals B, `0xc3e40e5e`; 76 `nand`+`nop-C`: nand(A equals B, A or not B) = `0x3c1bf1a1`; 80 `swap`; 82 `IO` writes it. Plain logic: **A xor B**, by way of EQU.
148	- **EQU** (low seed 3, 28 programs): 43 `nand`: nand(B, A) (pushed at 44); not A by arithmetic as for NOR (57, 60, 63, 65); B read at 66; 75, 78 `nand`: A or B; 90 `pop` (the stack chosen by `swap-stk` at 54 and 88); 91 `nand`: nand(not (A and B), A or B) = `0xc3e40e5e`; 92 `IO` writes it. Plain logic: **A equals B**, bit by bit.
149	
150	## 4. What it depends on in the Avida execution environment (c)
151	
152	Each test ran the same instruction sequences (letters unchanged) in the test processor with one thing of the Avida execution environment changed. Counted over the sequences that replicate and perform the task unchanged; "predicted" is the task set the replay computes from each program's own trace with the change applied along the same executed path, made before and independently of the run.
153	
154	| change | NOT | NAND | AND | ORN | OR | ANDN | NOR | XOR | EQU |
155	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
156	| none | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% |
157	| the `nand` letter means `nor` | 79% | 21% | 57% | 17% | 2% | 76% | 84% | 71% | 19% |
158	| the `nand` letter means `and` | 18% | 1% | 73% | 0% | 0% | 20% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
159	| `IO` means nothing (`nop-X`) | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
160	| other inputs of the world's kind, 3 triples | 99-100% | 100% | 99% | 99-100% | 99-100% | 100% | 99-100% | 100% | 100% |
161	| random 32-bit inputs | 85% | 90% | 66% | 77% | 85% | 80% | 84% | 87% | 71% |
162	| the fixed inputs in another order | 98% | 99% | 87% | 90% | 98% | 98% | 99% | 98% | 98% |
163	| the 26 meanings given to the letters in another order, 3 shufflings | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
164	
165	- **The meaning of the logic instruction.** With `nand` read as `nor`, 98% to 99% of the programs still replicate, and what they then perform is what their circuits compute with `nor` in place of `nand`: the prediction from the trace matches the test processor for 81,567 of 82,347 program-task pairs (99.1%). Where a circuit is `nand` alone, the task moves to its dual (NAND programs perform NOR: 97%); where arithmetic or a doubled input is in the circuit, it may stay (NOT of x via `nor(x,x)` is still NOT: 79%). With `and`, the prediction matches for 78,782 of 79,266 (99.4%).
166	- **The input and output channel.** With `IO` doing nothing, no program performs any task; 83% to 89% still replicate (`IO` is not part of their replication).
167	- **The numbers handed in.** Inputs of the kind Avida hands out in its worlds (the top 8 bits `0x0f`, `0x33`, `0x55`, the rest random): 99% to 100% still perform each task, and the trace prediction matches for 99.99%. Fully random 32-bit inputs: 66% to 90%, and 88% to 93% still replicate; the prediction along the same path matches for 88% (67,517 of 76,805). The difference: most programs' control instructions read numbers made from the inputs (for example comparisons by `if-less`), so other inputs change which instructions run; and circuits with carries give the task only on some inputs.
168	- **The whole instruction set.** With the 26 meanings reassigned (the three `nop` meanings among the letters a to c, the other 23 among d to z; Avida requires the `nop` instructions first), no program replicates or performs anything.
169	
170	So the same letters are a circuit for a task only given Avida's meanings for them, its `IO` channel and its rotation of inputs; given those, the circuit gives the task for most input numbers of the world's kind.
171	
172	## 5. What is left over (d)
173	
174	- **Not stopped by any ablation found**: 89 program-task pairs (NOT 45, ORN 44; 95 Avida programs, all in two runs), for which ablating every route site that leaves replication, and then every such site in the program, did not stop the task with replication left: their task's instructions (an `IO`, a `nand`, a mover) are all also required for replication (they sit in the replication loop). In two NOT programs the irreducible-set search found sets of size 3 (and 5, 6).
175	- **Redundancy**: 1,573 program-task pairs need a pair (section 2); the triples in the nine most common sequences show more minimal sets beyond the required instructions. The search is exhaustive only to pairs (to triples in nine sequences).
176	- **Required sites outside the route**: 17% of the required sites (rotation `IO`, stack switches, control, choices for instructions outside the route).
177	- **Route sites that are not required**: 15% (EQU) to 50% (NOT) of a credited route's sites: ablating them, the task is performed by another output.
178	- **Instructions outside every circuit**: over the 14,719 performing sequences' 1,459,777 sites: 437,714 (30%) are in some route of some task (5,477 of these also required for replication), 230,290 (16%) are required for replication only, 720,706 (49%) are executed but in no route and not required for replication, 71,067 (5%) are never executed.
179	- **Replication-required sites**: their ablation stops the task's credit in 80% of cases (1,081,852 of 1,359,165), because the program no longer splits (a program that never splits is credited nothing); in the traces of each run's most common sequence with one replication-required site ablated, the task outputs are still written in most cases (all tasks in 125 of 159 such traces, some in 24, none in 10). They are part of what stops the credit, not part of the circuit.
180	- **Programs credited without replicating**: 1,549 sequences (1,552 Avida programs) split but do not replicate and are still credited with tasks; each of them has, for each of its tasks, a single site whose ablation stops the credit. They are outside the counts of sections 2 to 4.
181	- **Circuits not computable on all eight combinations**: those holding a constant folded as OTHER (100 of NOT's 350 reduced circuits; 7 to 40 for the others); the generality check (200 input triples, computed on the actual numbers) covers them.
182	- **The trace reading itself**: 0 steps where the replay's number differs from Avida's trace; 0 disagreements between the first accepted output and the trace's own credit.
183	
184	## 6. Departures from the plan
185	
186	1. **The trace reader's circuit form.** The first reader wrote each circuit as one nested expression; in programs whose parts are used many times it grew without bound (one worker passed 1.6 GB of memory; an earlier pool broke), and the job was stopped by its exact process numbers. The reader now keeps each circuit as a table of distinct parts (identical parts merged, as the plan asks), works without recursion, folds `nand` with ZERO to ONES in the reduced form, and records each part's logic id. The first run's output from the old reader was set aside unread for results.
187	2. **The shuffled instruction sets (E4)**: Avida refused a set with the `nop` instructions anywhere ("invalid NOP placement"); the shufflings keep the three `nop` meanings among a to c and shuffle the other 23. A few letters keep their meaning by chance (2 to 4 per shuffling).
188	3. **Replication and credit.** The plan says a program that never splits is credited nothing; that holds, but Avida's "viable" means forming a colony, and 1,549 sequences split without replicating and are credited. They are counted apart (section 5). The environment tests are counted over the same replicating performers as the ablations.
189	4. **Added, not planned**: the world's own counts (section 1); the required sites against the credited route; the bit-by-bit check of every reduced circuit on all eight combinations and the grouping by the functions their parts compute; the naming of roles outside the routes (rotation `IO`, stack switch); three reruns in the scratch space for the worked examples (the NOT example's `IO` at 11 and 26, the EQU example's `IO` at 45).
190	5. **Run times**: the pairs took two workers and a four-hour limit (the plan said about 1.5 hours on three); the last run's traces were read again with three workers after one worker went slowly (its programs write many outputs). Nothing else changed.
191	
192	## 7. Tested, not tested, unsure
193	
194	**Tested**: every single ablation of every distinct instruction sequence; every pair among the sites that leave replication, in every replicating performer; triples in the nine most common; Avida's trace of every sequence, replayed with no differing step; the circuits' outputs checked against Avida's task check, on the fixed inputs, on all eight bit combinations, and on 200 other input triples; four kinds of change to the Avida execution environment, with predictions made from the traces.
195	
196	**Not tested**: ablation by deleting an instruction (which shifts every later position) rather than replacing it by `nop-X`; sets of three or more beyond the greedy search (outside the nine most common sequences); task performance outside the test processor (in the world, with neighbours and changing inputs); whether the circuits found are the only ones a program could execute on other inputs (the traces follow one run, on the fixed inputs).
197	
198	**Unsure**: the canonical form names parts by a hash, so two circuits could in principle share a form by collision (not seen; 20 hexadecimal digits); "the same circuit" here means the same operations on the same inputs after identity steps are dropped, and circuits with the same bit-by-bit result but different arithmetic count as different; the role of a required site outside the route is read from what it was executed as, not tested one by one (three reruns only).
199	
200

# S112 What the evolved sums are: what had to be removed, and what it is

*Log S112, decisions S60 and S61. Written 30 September 2026 by the one Opus 5.5 agent of log S112 (S56), after the runs, **before the GLM cross-examination**. In the owner's Avida terms (S61, `records/Semantics - Avida terms, given by the owner.md`): an **Avida program** is one program in a program population; a **distinct instruction sequence** is what the plan called a genotype (every Avida program with the same instructions); a **logic task** (the owner's "rudimentary math", the plan's "sum") is one of Avida's nine: NOT, NAND, AND, ORN, OR, ANDN, NOR, XOR, EQU; **task performance** is Avida's test processor crediting the task; **instruction ablation** replaces one instruction by `nop-X`, which does nothing. All entities are digital programs executing on Avida's virtual CPU; nothing biological is involved. The plan, written before running: `results/S112 What the evolved sums are - how it will be found, written before running.md`. The numbers: the `.json` beside this file, written by `tools/s112_summarise_what_had_to_be_removed_and_what_it_is.py`. The exact commands, with every departure: `results/S112 What the evolved sums are - the runs/the exact commands.txt`. Raw output (traces, ablation lists) stays in the scratch space. Observations only; nothing is settled (S28). Nothing in the theory, Part A, Part B, S110 or S111 is written.*

---

## 0. The answer, in short

The owner asked two things (S60): what had to be removed from the Avida programs that did the logic tasks for them to stop, and what that evolved information is, given the Avida execution environment.

**What had to be removed.** For each task, in 98.0% of the program-task pairs (98.6% counted by Avida program) among the programs that perform it and replicate, **one instruction** is enough: there are sites whose single ablation stops the task performance while program replication goes on. These are the program's **required instructions** for that task: on average 5 (NOT, NAND) to 27 (XOR) per program. They are, by kind, mostly `IO` (the instruction that writes a number out and reads the next number in), `nand` (the one logic instruction), `nop-C` and `nop-A` placed right after an instruction (they choose which register it acts on), `swap`, `push`, `pop` (they move numbers between registers and stacks), and for some tasks `add`, `sub`, `inc`, `dec`. By role on Avida's virtual CPU: the reads of the input numbers, the `nand` steps and arithmetic that combine them, the moves and register choices that wire one step to the next, the output write, and **extra `IO` reads that are not on the path at all but set which input number the later reads receive** (Avida hands the three input numbers out in rotation). In the other 2.0%: 1,573 needed a pair of sites (almost always the task has a second route that one ablation leaves standing), two needed a set of three, and 89 (NOT and ORN only, 95 Avida programs) could not be made to stop by ablation while replicating, because every instruction of their task is also an instruction of their replication.

**What it is.** In the Avida execution environment, what those instructions make up, when executed, is a **small fixed circuit of the instruction set's operations** from the input reads to the output write: a few `nand` steps, sometimes with `add`, `sub`, `inc`, `dec` steps that on these numbers act bit by bit, applied to the numbers the `IO` channel hands in. For example, the most common circuit of NOT is one `nand` of an input with itself (63% of the NOT programs); of NAND, one `nand` of two inputs (82%); of ORN, `nand(nand(x,y),x)` (69%); of EQU, a five- to eight-step circuit (four circuits cover 81% of the EQU programs). Across all 23,332 distinct instruction sequences of the nine runs, each task has from 35 (XOR) to 409 (OR) distinct circuits (identity steps removed), but a few are run by most programs, and each common circuit is realised by many different instruction strings (the top NOT circuit by 347 different strings of route instructions, in 7,925 distinct sequences). Every circuit that could be computed on all eight combinations of input bits (all but those holding an unnamed constant) gives an output Avida's check accepts for its task, save one.

**What it depends on.** It is that circuit only with Avida's meanings for the letters: read the `nand` letter as `nor` and 2% to 84% of the programs still perform a given task, while the rest perform what the circuit then computes (predicted from the trace for 99% of the programs); read it as `and` and 0% to 73% remain; read `IO` as doing nothing and no task is performed by any program; give the 26 letters other meanings and no program replicates or performs anything. With other input numbers of the kind Avida hands out in its worlds, 99% to 100% still perform each task; with fully random 32-bit numbers, 66% to 90%.

The rest of this file gives the numbers, the method, worked examples and what is left over.

## 1. The programs

- **All distinct instruction sequences alive** at update 50,000 in the nine S111 runs (three copy error rates, three seeds): **23,332 sequences, 32,193 Avida programs** (read from each run's `detail-50000.spop`).
- Each was run alone in Avida's test processor on Avida's fixed inputs (`0x0f13149f`, `0x3308e53e`, `0x556241eb`, called A, B and C below; every combination of three bits occurs among their 32 bit places). **14,965 sequences (23,813 programs) replicate** in the test processor (Avida's "viable": the copy is exact, or leads back to the program, `cTestCPU.cc` 282-313); **14,719 of them (23,553 programs) perform at least one task**. 8,367 sequences do not replicate; 1,549 of these (1,552 programs) still split off a copy and are credited with tasks (Avida credits the tasks of the last split, `cAnalyzeGenotype.cc` 590); they are counted apart (section 6).
- Every count is given by distinct instruction sequence and, where it matters, by Avida program.

| task | sequences performing it (replicating) | Avida programs | share of all 32,193 programs | programs Avida's world counted as performing it at update 50,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NOT | 12,732 | 21,366 | 66.4% | 29,440 |
| NAND | 12,161 | 20,717 | 64.3% | 28,413 |
| AND | 7,246 | 11,849 | 36.8% | 17,614 |
| ORN | 12,159 | 20,802 | 64.6% | 29,043 |
| OR | 10,566 | 19,077 | 59.3% | 27,164 |
| ANDN | 11,214 | 19,778 | 61.4% | 28,040 |
| NOR | 9,590 | 18,045 | 56.0% | 26,120 |
| XOR | 2,673 | 5,782 | 18.0% | 8,652 |
| EQU | 5,384 | 10,765 | 33.4% | 16,131 |

The world's counts are higher, as S111 found; S111 left the reason unchecked, and it is not checked here either.

## 2. What had to be removed (a)

**How.** Every single site of every sequence was ablated (2,330,137 Avida programs run); every pair of sites whose single ablation leaves replication was ablated in every replicating sequence that performs a task (52,428,814 programs run); for the 91 program-task pairs with no stopping set of one or two sites, the irreducible-set search of the plan; for the most common sequence of each run, every triple (836,544 programs run). A set **stops a task** if, with it ablated, the program still replicates in the test processor and the task is no longer credited. A set is **minimal** if no smaller part of it stops the task.

**The smallest set that stops each task:**

| task | size 1 (sequences) | size 2 | size 3 or more | none found | size 1, by Avida programs | required instructions per sequence: mean (range) | distinct strings of required instructions |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NOT | 12,014 | 671 | 2 | 45 | 95.5% | 5.2 (0-31) | 1,704 |
| NAND | 11,698 | 463 | 0 | 0 | 97.2% | 5.3 (0-23) | 705 |
| AND | 7,239 | 7 | 0 | 0 | 99.9% | 12.7 (0-34) | 1,184 |
| ORN | 11,850 | 265 | 0 | 44 | 98.4% | 7.1 (0-29) | 1,676 |
| OR | 10,565 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 100.0% | 13.0 (0-29) | 1,361 |
| ANDN | 11,048 | 166 | 0 | 0 | 99.1% | 10.3 (0-36) | 1,553 |
| NOR | 9,590 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 100% | 15.8 (3-36) | 1,639 |
| XOR | 2,673 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 100% | 27.0 (18-38) | 458 |
| EQU | 5,384 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 100% | 21.9 (7-33) | 742 |

Over the nine tasks, 82,061 of 83,725 program-task pairs (98.0%) are stopped by one site. The **required instructions** of a program for a task are the sites whose single ablation stops it; the table's "0" minimum is the programs stopped only by pairs.

**What the required instructions are, by kind** (share of all required sites, over all sequences):

| task | IO | nand | nop-C | swap | nop-A | others above 2% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NOT | 31% | 16% | 18% | 11% | 3% | dec 4%, pop 3%, inc 2%, if-less 2% |
| NAND | 38% | 19% | 23% | 9% | 4% | if-label 3% |
| AND | 30% | 17% | 16% | 9% | 4% | inc 5%, add 5%, pop 3%, if-less 3% |
| ORN | 40% | 21% | 17% | 9% | 3% | if-less 3%, sub 2%, dec 2% |
| OR | 28% | 22% | 20% | 8% | 7% | sub 3%, add 3%, if-label 2%, dec 2% |
| ANDN | 24% | 18% | 20% | 6% | 3% | add 8%, inc 7%, pop 4%, sub 3% |
| NOR | 26% | 19% | 18% | 7% | 6% | add 5%, pop 3%, sub 3%, inc 3% |
| XOR | 24% | 22% | 21% | 7% | 5% | push 5%, pop 5%, swap-stk 3%, sub 2% |
| EQU | 31% | 20% | 20% | 7% | 5% | push 4%, pop 4%, sub 3%, swap-stk 2% |

**By role**, read from Avida's trace of the unablated program (section 3), weighted by Avida programs: for every task the largest roles are the **register choices** (the `nop` read right after an instruction, which picks the register it acts on: 16% to 24%), the **gates** (`nand`: 14% to 21%), the **input reads** (`IO` that brings in a number the circuit uses: 10% to 23%), the **movers** (`swap`, `push`, `pop`: 7% to 16%), **arithmetic** (`add`, `sub`, `inc`, `dec` on the path: 3% to 18%), the **output write** (3% to 13%), and **`IO` outside the routes** (1% to 11%): an `IO` whose own input and output are not on the path, but which takes the next number of Avida's input rotation (`cPopulationCell.h` 214-218: each `IO` reads the next of the three numbers in turn), so that removing it shifts which number every later read receives. Control instructions (`if-less`, `if-label`, `h-search`, jumps) are 1% to 6%, and register or head choices of instructions outside the routes 2% to 9%.

**Required instructions against the route.** 83% of all required sites (a sum over the nine tasks: 751,212 of 904,433) lie in the credited route (the output Avida credits and the instructions that made it, section 3); the other 17% are the `IO` reads that set the rotation, stack switches, control instructions and register choices of instructions outside the route. In the other direction, 50% (NOT) to 85% (EQU) of a credited route's sites are required: the rest can be ablated and the task is performed anyway, most often because another output then carries it (an example in section 2.1).

**What the programs share across runs.** The same kinds and roles, in every run (the two tables above). On Avida's virtual CPU a route's required instructions execute in one order: input reads (with the rotation-setting `IO` among them), then gates and arithmetic with their register choices and the movers between them, then the output write (every worked example in section 3.1 runs so; their positions in the instruction sequence were not compared across all programs). The exact strings differ: 458 (XOR) to 1,704 (NOT) distinct strings of required instructions, in the order of the instruction sequence, for 2,673 to 12,732 sequences.

**Redundancy.** Of the 1,664 program-task pairs that no single site stops, 1,646 have more than one route in the trace (NOT 712 of 718, NAND 452 of 463, ORN 308 of 309, ANDN 166 of 166, AND 7 of 7, OR 1 of 1); a minimal pair then takes out one site of each route (or of the rotation and one route). Pairs also exist beside single sites: minimal pairs total 876,577 over all tasks and programs, in addition to the required instructions. In the most common sequence of each run, exhaustive triples found further minimal sets of size 3 (0 to 254 per task: in default seed 1's, 254 for NOT). So the required instructions are the smallest removals, not the only ones.

### 2.1 Worked examples of what had to be removed

**NOT, low seed 2's most common NOT sequence (44 Avida programs, 110 instructions).** Its route (Avida's trace): site 11 `IO` reads B into register BX; site 12 `push` puts it on the stack; site 16 `pop` (with `nop-C` at 17) puts it into CX; site 20 `nand` computes nand(BX, CX) = nand(B, B) = NOT B into BX; site 21 `swap` moves it to CX; site 26 `IO` (with `nop-C` at 27) writes CX out, which Avida's check accepts as NOT. **Required** (single ablation stops NOT, replication goes on): site 12 `push`, 15 `nop-C` (the register choice of the instruction before it), 20 `nand`, 21 `swap`, 27 `nop-C`. **Not required although on the route**: the input read at 11 (with it ablated, an earlier `IO` in the rotation supplies a number, and NOT of any input is NOT) and the output write at 26 (with it ablated, the NOT value stays in CX and a later `IO`, at site 34, writes out a three-`nand` NOT circuit instead: rerun in the scratch space). So for NOT, what had to be removed is the `nand` that makes it and the wiring that brings one number to both of its operands and its result to the output register. Nine minimal pairs exist beside these five (for example the two `IO` at sites 10 and 11 together).

**EQU, low seed 3's most common EQU sequence (28 Avida programs, 108 instructions).** Required: 25 sites: `IO` at 27, 41, 47, 53, 66 (input reads), `IO` at 45, 51, 55 (outside the route: rotation), `nand` at 43, 75, 78, 91, `add` 60, `inc` 63, `sub` 65, `push` 44, `pop` 90, `swap-stk` 54 and 88 (they decide which stack the `pop` reads), `nop-C` at 28, 61, 67, 76, 79 (register choices), and the output `IO` at 92. No minimal pair. Ablating the rotation `IO` at 45 (rerun): the later reads at 47, 53, 66 get C, B, A instead of A, C, B, and the output at 92 becomes another function (logic id 139), not EQU.

## 3. What it is: the circuits (b)

**How.** Avida's own `TRACE` of every sequence on the fixed inputs (analysis mode). A replay follows each trace step by step and carries, for every register and stack place, where its number came from (an input read, a constant, or an operation on earlier numbers), using the register and stack effects of each instruction in Avida's source (`cHardwareCPU.cc`); after every step the carried numbers are compared with the trace. **Steps where the replay's number differs from Avida's trace: 0**, in all 23,332 sequences. Each output an `IO` writes is put to Avida's check (the logic id rule, `cTaskLib.cc` 369-448, with the lists each task accepts, 513-575); every accepted output is a **route** for the task; the first is the one Avida credits, and for **every** performing sequence and task it is the step at which the trace's own task count goes from 0 to 1 (83,725 of 83,725). The tasks the trace credits equal the test processor's for all 14,965 replicating sequences.

**The circuit** of a route: the operations from the output back to the input reads, with the movers and register choices left out as wires, constant parts folded to ZERO, ONES (all 32 bits set) or OTHER, identical parts merged, and the three inputs named x0, x1, x2 in the order that gives the smallest written form (so the same circuit on other inputs counts once). The **reduced** form also drops steps that leave a number unchanged (`add` or `sub` of ZERO, `inc` after `dec`, `dec` after `inc`) and writes `nand` with ONES as a `nand` of the number with itself, and `nand` with ZERO as ONES. Each reduced circuit was also computed on the three numbers `0x0f0f0f0f`, `0x33333333`, `0x55555555` (every byte holds all eight combinations of three bits) to read which bit-by-bit function each of its parts is.

Grouped by the set of bit-by-bit functions their parts compute (whatever instructions compute them), the reduced circuits fall into 16 (XOR) to 283 (OR) groups.

### 3.1 One worked example per task, in the instruction set's terms and in plain logic

A, B, C are Avida's fixed inputs `0x0f13149f`, `0x3308e53e`, `0x556241eb`; AX, BX, CX the three registers; each line is one executed instruction from Avida's trace, with its site (position in the instruction sequence). - **AND** (low seed 1, 27 programs): 39 `IO` reads C into BX; 40 `IO`+`nop-C` reads A into CX; 42 `nand`: nand(C, A) = `0xfafdff74`; 43 `nand`: nand(that, A) = `0xf5eeebeb` (not A or C); 45 `add` A: `0x0502008a`; 47 `inc`: `0x0502008b`; 53 `IO` writes it. Plain logic: **A and C** (`0x0f13149f and 0x556241eb = 0x0502008b`).
- **ORN** (low seed 2, 44 programs): B into BX (11, 12, 16, 21); 26 `IO`+`nop-C` reads C into CX; 28 `nand`+`nop-C`: CX := nand(B, C) = `0xeeffbed5`; 30 `nand`+`nop-C`: CX := nand(B, that) = `0xddf75beb`; 34 `IO`+`nop-C` writes it. Plain logic: **C or not B**.
- **OR** (default seed 1, 12 programs): 33 `IO`+`nop-C` reads A into CX; 41 and 45 `IO` (outside the route: rotation); 47 `IO` reads A into BX; 48 `IO`+`nop-A` reads B into AX; 52 `nand`: BX := nand(A, A) = not A; 61 `swap`+`nop-C` brings B into CX; 63 `nand`+`nop-C`: CX := nand(not A, B) = A or not B; 65 `nand`+`nop-A`: AX := nand(not A, A or not B) = `0x3f1bf5bf`; 69 and 73 `swap`; 78 `IO`+`nop-A` writes AX. Plain logic: **A or B**.
- **ANDN** (low seed 3, 28 programs): 47 `IO`+`nop-C` reads A into CX; 53 `IO` reads C into BX; 57 `nand`: nand(C, A); 60 `add`+`nop-C`: CX := that + A; 63 `inc`+`nop-C`: `0x0a111414`; 66 `IO`+`nop-C` writes it. Plain logic: **A and not C**.
- **NOR** (low seed 3, 28 programs): A and C read (47, 53); 57 `nand`, 60 `add`, 63 `inc`, 65 `sub`: BX := nand(C, A) − (A and not C) = `0xf0eceb60` = not A; 66 `IO`+`nop-C` reads B; 75 `nand`: A or not B; 78 `nand`: A or B = `0x3f1bf5bf`; 81 `push`, 83 `pop`; 85 `nand`: nand(A or B, A or B) = `0xc0e40a40`; 89 `IO` writes it. Plain logic: **not (A or B)**; C enters and cancels.
- **XOR** (default seed 1, 12 programs): 43 `nand`: nand(B, A) (pushed at 44); not A (52), A or not B (63), A or B (65) as for OR; 71 `pop`; 72 `nand`: nand(not (A and B), A or B) = A equals B, `0xc3e40e5e`; 76 `nand`+`nop-C`: nand(A equals B, A or not B) = `0x3c1bf1a1`; 80 `swap`; 82 `IO` writes it. - **EQU** (low seed 3, 28 programs): 43 `nand`: nand(B, A) (pushed at 44); not A by arithmetic as for NOR (57, 60, 63, 65); B read at 66; 75, 78 `nand`: A or B; 90 `pop` (the stack chosen by `swap-stk` at 54 and 88); 91 `nand`: nand(not (A and B), A or B) = `0xc3e40e5e`; 92 `IO` writes it. Plain logic: **A equals B**, bit by bit.

## 4. What it depends on in the Avida execution environment (c)

Each test ran the same instruction sequences (letters unchanged) in the test processor with one thing of the Avida execution environment changed. Counted over the sequences that replicate and perform the task unchanged; "predicted" is the task set the replay computes from each program's own trace with the change applied along the same executed path, made before and independently of the run.

| change | NOT | NAND | AND | ORN | OR | ANDN | NOR | XOR | EQU |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| the `nand` letter means `nor` | 79% | 21% | 57% | 17% | 2% | 76% | 84% | 71% | 19% |
| the `nand` letter means `and` | 18% | 1% | 73% | 0% | 0% | 20% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| `IO` means nothing (`nop-X`) | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| other inputs of the world's kind, 3 triples | 99-100% | 100% | 99% | 99-100% | 99-100% | 100% | 99-100% | 100% | 100% |
| random 32-bit inputs | 85% | 90% | 66% | 77% | 85% | 80% | 84% | 87% | 71% |
| the fixed inputs in another order | 98% | 99% | 87% | 90% | 98% | 98% | 99% | 98% | 98% |
| the 26 meanings given to the letters in another order, 3 shufflings | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% |

- **The meaning of the logic instruction.** With `nand` read as `nor`, 98% to 99% of the programs still replicate, and what they then perform is what their circuits compute with `nor` in place of `nand`: the prediction from the trace matches the test processor for 81,567 of 82,347 program-task pairs (99.1%). Where a circuit is `nand` alone, the task moves to its dual (NAND programs perform NOR: 97%); where arithmetic or a doubled input is in the circuit, it may stay (NOT of x via `nor(x,x)` is still NOT: 79%). With `and`, the prediction matches for 78,782 of 79,266 (99.4%).
- **The input and output channel.** With `IO` doing nothing, no program performs any task; 83% to 89% still replicate (`IO` is not part of their replication).
- **The numbers handed in.** Inputs of the kind Avida hands out in its worlds (the top 8 bits `0x0f`, `0x33`, `0x55`, the rest random): 99% to 100% still perform each task, and the trace prediction matches for 99.99%. Fully random 32-bit inputs: 66% to 90%, and 88% to 93% still replicate; the prediction along the same path matches for 88% (67,517 of 76,805). The difference: most programs' control instructions read numbers made from the inputs (for example comparisons by `if-less`), so other inputs change which instructions run; and circuits with carries give the task only on some inputs.
- **The whole instruction set.** With the 26 meanings reassigned (the three `nop` meanings among the letters a to c, the other 23 among d to z; Avida requires the `nop` instructions first), no program replicates or performs anything.

So the same letters are a circuit for a task only given Avida's meanings for them, its `IO` channel and its rotation of inputs; given those, the circuit gives the task for most input numbers of the world's kind.

## 5. What is left over (d)

- **Not stopped by any ablation found**: 89 program-task pairs (NOT 45, ORN 44; 95 Avida programs, all in two runs), for which ablating every route site that leaves replication, and then every such site in the program, did not stop the task with replication left: their task's instructions (an `IO`, a `nand`, a mover) are all also required for replication (they sit in the replication loop). In two NOT programs the irreducible-set search found sets of size 3 (and 5, 6).
- **Redundancy**: 1,573 program-task pairs need a pair (section 2); the triples in the nine most common sequences show more minimal sets beyond the required instructions. The search is exhaustive only to pairs (to triples in nine sequences).
- **Required sites outside the route**: 17% of the required sites (rotation `IO`, stack switches, control, choices for instructions outside the route).
- **Route sites that are not required**: 15% (EQU) to 50% (NOT) of a credited route's sites: ablating them, the task is performed by another output.
- **Instructions outside every circuit**: over the 14,719 performing sequences' 1,459,777 sites: 437,714 (30%) are in some route of some task (5,477 of these also required for replication), 230,290 (16%) are required for replication only, 720,706 (49%) are executed but in no route and not required for replication, 71,067 (5%) are never executed.
- **Replication-required sites**: their ablation stops the task's credit in 80% of cases (1,081,852 of 1,359,165), because the program no longer splits (a program that never splits is credited nothing); in the traces of each run's most common sequence with one replication-required site ablated, the task outputs are still written in most cases (all tasks in 125 of 159 such traces, some in 24, none in 10). They are part of what stops the credit, not part of the circuit.
- **Programs credited without replicating**: 1,549 sequences (1,552 Avida programs) split but do not replicate and are still credited with tasks; each of them has, for each of its tasks, a single site whose ablation stops the credit. They are outside the counts of sections 2 to 4.
- **Circuits not computable on all eight combinations**: those holding a constant folded as OTHER (100 of NOT's 350 reduced circuits; 7 to 40 for the others); the generality check (200 input triples, computed on the actual numbers) covers them.
- **The trace reading itself**: 0 steps where the replay's number differs from Avida's trace; 0 disagreements between the first accepted output and the trace's own credit.

## 6. Departures from the plan

1. **The trace reader's circuit form.** The first reader wrote each circuit as one nested expression; in programs whose parts are used many times it grew without bound (one worker passed 1.6 GB of memory; an earlier pool broke), and the job was stopped by its exact process numbers. The reader now keeps each circuit as a table of distinct parts (identical parts merged, as the plan asks), works without recursion, folds `nand` with ZERO to ONES in the reduced form, and records each part's logic id. The first run's output from the old reader was set aside unread for results.
2. **The shuffled instruction sets (E4)**: Avida refused a set with the `nop` instructions anywhere ("invalid NOP placement"); the shufflings keep the three `nop` meanings among a to c and shuffle the other 23. A few letters keep their meaning by chance (2 to 4 per shuffling).
3. **Replication and credit.** The plan says a program that never splits is credited nothing; that holds, but Avida's "viable" means forming a colony, and 1,549 sequences split without replicating and are credited. They are counted apart (section 5). The environment tests are counted over the same replicating performers as the ablations.
4. **Added, not planned**: the world's own counts (section 1); the required sites against the credited route; the bit-by-bit check of every reduced circuit on all eight combinations and the grouping by the functions their parts compute; the naming of roles outside the routes (rotation `IO`, stack switch); three reruns in the scratch space for the worked examples (the NOT example's `IO` at 11 and 26, the EQU example's `IO` at 45).
5. **Run times**: the pairs took two workers and a four-hour limit (the plan said about 1.5 hours on three); the last run's traces were read again with three workers after one worker went slowly (its programs write many outputs). Nothing else changed.

## 7. Tested, not tested, unsure

**Tested**: every single ablation of every distinct instruction sequence; every pair among the sites that leave replication, in every replicating performer; triples in the nine most common; Avida's trace of every sequence, replayed with no differing step; the circuits' outputs checked against Avida's task check, on the fixed inputs, on all eight bit combinations, and on 200 other input triples; four kinds of change to the Avida execution environment, with predictions made from the traces.

**Not tested**: ablation by deleting an instruction (which shifts every later position) rather than replacing it by `nop-X`; sets of three or more beyond the greedy search (outside the nine most common sequences); task performance outside the test processor (in the world, with neighbours and changing inputs); whether the circuits found are the only ones a program could execute on other inputs (the traces follow one run, on the fixed inputs).

**Unsure**: the canonical form names parts by a hash, so two circuits could in principle share a form by collision (not seen; 20 hexadecimal digits); "the same circuit" here means the same operations on the same inputs after identity steps are dropped, and circuits with the same bit-by-bit result but different arithmetic count as different; the role of a required site outside the route is read from what it was executed as, not tested one by one (three reruns only).

1	# S112 What the evolved sums are: how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending
2	
3	*Written 30 September 2026 by the one Opus 5.5 agent that does the whole S112 job under decision S56 (the plan, the instruction ablations, the traces, the execution-environment tests, the results and the plain-words file), before anything of this cross-examination was built or sent. When this file was committed, the returns folder `results/S112 What the evolved sums are - GLM cross-examination returns/` did not exist, no brief or manifest had been built, no call had been sent and no runner of it was going. It follows log S111's cross-examination rule (`results/S111 Avida - how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending.md`) where it says nothing else. It is written in the owner's Avida terms (decision S61, `records/Semantics - Avida terms, given by the owner.md`). It obeys decision S23 except where it quotes the owner; for what the theory judges it says "candidate" or "explanation", never "model" (S43).*
4	
5	## The instruction
6	
7	- **S56**, the owner's words: "It's capable of doing the whole thing on its own. Use GLM for cross examination." So one Opus agent does the whole S112 job, and GLM cross-examines it in place of a fresh Opus critical reviewer.
8	- **S60**: the job itself, in the owner's words: "Of the of machines that could do rudimentary math, what needed to be removed in order for them to stop doing that math. Ignore the fact that they were evolved to solve a problem, I want to know what that evolved information actually is, given the environment it was instantiated in." **S61**: the owner's Avida terms, used in every file, brief and reply of this log.
9	- **S39, S29, S17**: up to four GLM calls at once, each through Claude Code, at medium effort. **S20, S21, S23, S28, S43**: the owner's words bind every finding as content. Part B stays held before its settlement (S57); nothing of Part B, S110 or S111 is written.
10	
11	## What is sent
12	
13	Four jobs, built by `tools/s112x_build.py` (log S111's build with its names, files and briefs changed; Part A round 1's build imported for its helpers only; the sandboxed helper `tools/glm_via_claude_code_sandboxed.py` and the shell guard `tools/glm_sandbox_shell_guard.py` used unchanged), run by `tools/s112x_glm_loop.py` (log S111's runner with its names changed):
14	
15	| job | tag | angle |
16	|---|---|---|
17	| 1 | `s112x_glm_a` | (a) whether the answer answers the owner's two questions exactly |
18	| 2 | `s112x_glm_b` | (b) the minimal-removal search (instruction ablation) and its limits |
19	| 3 | `s112x_glm_c` | (c) the circuits and their canonical forms against the traces |
20	| 4 | `s112x_glm_d` | (d) the plain-words file against the results |
21	
22	Each sandbox holds copies only: the plan written before running (with its dated note on the terms); the results (`.md`, `.json`); the plain-words file 112; this rule; the owner's Avida terms; the exact commands; log S111's Avida configuration files and its build notes (Avida's rules as read from its source); the five S112 scripts (the test-processor helper, the trace reader, the minimal-removal search, the execution-environment tests, the summariser). Job 1 adds the decisions record and S111's results after its cross-examination; job 4 adds the decisions record and plain file 111 (for style). **No sandbox holds Avida's source or binary, or any raw output** (traces, ablation lists, saved program populations): those stay in the scratch space, and the build refuses any source outside `Semantics/`. There is no program in any sandbox (no `model/` folder), so the guard refuses every command: GLM may Read, Glob and Grep, and writes nothing. Each brief quotes the owner's words (S20, S21, S23, S28, S43, S56, S60, S61) and asks for objections, each with **the exact fix**, terse, at most about 3,000 words, last line `END OF REPORT`. The briefs, manifests and job list are named, with their md5s, in `tools/s112x_jobs - S112, GLM cross-examination.json`, written by the build and committed before the launch.
23	
24	- **The call**: glm-5.3 through Claude Code (S29), `--effort medium` (S17), the 1,000,000-token window, 6 attempts, at most 3 answers without END OF REPORT, 7,200 seconds per attempt, `--rule` (this file, committed and unchanged from HEAD), `--brief-md5`, `--manifest-md5`. Up to 3 passes per job. Sandboxes in `<scratchpad>/s112x_sandboxes/`, homes in `<scratchpad>/s112x_homes/`. Returns in `results/S112 What the evolved sums are - GLM cross-examination returns/`.
25	- **Before the launch**: a dry test of the four sandboxes with a dummy key (built by the helper's own `build_sandbox`; the guard handed a write, `touch`, two `python3 -c`, `cat`, `env`, a redirect and a run of one of the S112 scripts, each to be refused; every sandbox to come back unchanged; no Avida binary, no `.spop`, `.dat`, `.trace` or `.jsonl` file, no file larger than 400,000 bytes), recorded and committed; no other GLM run of this project going, so that no more than four GLM calls run at once.
26	
27	## How the replies will be read
28	
29	1. **Nothing is opened until all four calls end.** No reply, receipt, reasoning file, attempt file, stream file or guard log of this cross-examination is opened until every job has ended its last allowed pass: the run log holds `s112x_glm_loop: every pass ended; …` and `loop ended <UTC time>`, and the process in the pid file has exited. The progress lines may be watched; they hold no reply text. If a call is still running 24 hours after the launch, the runner may be stopped by its PID and the calls not ended recorded as not returned.
30	2. **What counts as a reply**: only `<tag>.response.txt` (or `<tag>_pass<k>.response.txt`); failed calls count neither way; connection failures are not answers; a key in the output or a sandbox not unchanged is reported before anything else is read.
31	3. **One Opus agent reads every objection and settles each**, by argument from the plan, the results, the scripts, the configuration and Avida's source, or **by rerunning** (Avida in analysis mode, the scripts, or a new check) in the scratch space (`/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-ThreadSmith/8d9323da-c0ec-57ec-91fd-8f99ca99320a/scratchpad`), never in the repository; and records for each: the objection, its settlement (stands, stands in part, does not stand), the reason (or the rerun and its numbers), and what it changes. An objection is a claim until settled; an objection repeated by several jobs decides nothing (arguments, not numbers); silence is not agreement. The agent writes `results/S112 What the evolved sums are - the GLM cross-examination, settled.md`, created at once and filled as it goes.
32	4. **Findings that stand amend the S112 files in corrected copies**: `… , after the cross-examination.md` (and `.json`) beside the results file, and corrected copies of any script that changes (with its own plain name and note); the files as sent are kept as they were. The plain-words file 112 is updated to match, and its note says it now follows the check. Nothing in the theory's text, formal core, claims or program, any Part A, Part B, S110 or S111 file, the decisions record, the S61 terms file or `authority/` is written.
33	5. **The owner's words bind every finding as content** (S20 to S61). An objection that would settle for the owner something the S112 files leave open (whether what was found is knowledge; how the owner's question should be read beyond what S60 says) is recorded, not applied (S28, S21). No finding ranks anything (S20).
34	6. **Records** follow the settlement, by the same agent: an addition to log S112 in the project story and the plain story, and Status, INDEX and README as earlier entries did. Then the owner chooses the next step.
35	
36	## How the run is launched
37	
38	From the repository root, after this file's commit is pushed and the build and dry test are committed, one process, detached so that it outlives the agent that starts it, with the key loaded only into its own environment from the session's key file and never opened or printed by the agent, and the other keys unset:
39	
40	```
41	setsid nohup bash -c 'cd /home/user/ThreadSmith || exit 1; echo "launched $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"; R="Semantics/results/S112 What the evolved sums are - how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending.md"; { git ls-files --error-unmatch -- "$R" >/dev/null && git diff --quiet HEAD -- "$R"; } || { echo "the reading rule is not committed or differs from HEAD; nothing sent"; exit 1; }; set -a; . <key file>; set +a; unset ATRIA_API_KEY MIMO_API_KEY OPENAI_API_KEY; python3 -B Semantics/tools/s112x_glm_loop.py "Semantics/tools/s112x_jobs - S112, GLM cross-examination.json"; echo "loop ended $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"' > <scratchpad>/s112x_glm_run.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &
42	```
43	
44	The process id of the session leader goes in `<scratchpad>/s112x_glm_run.pid`. The launching agent writes `results/S112 What the evolved sums are - GLM cross-examination, launch record.md`, commits it, and hands back once the log shows all four calls sent.
45	
46	## Unsure
47	
48	- GLM cannot run Avida or see the traces or the ablation lists; it judges the numbers by their consistency with the scripts, the configuration, the worked examples and each other. A claim it cannot check is to be listed as not reached, not as an objection.
49	- GLM sees Avida's rules only as S111's build notes and the S112 scripts' citations give them; a rule misread there could pass unnoticed.
50	- One GLM job per angle may miss what the work also missed.
51	
52	Decided by Claude under decisions S17, S29, S39, S56, S60 and S61. 30 September 2026.
53

Each sandbox holds copies only: the plan written before running (with its dated note on the terms); the results (`.md`, `.json`); the plain-words file 112; this rule; the owner's Avida terms; the exact commands; log S111's Avida configuration files and its build notes (Avida's rules as read from its source); the five S112 scripts (the test-processor helper, the trace reader, the minimal-removal search, the execution-environment tests, the summariser). Job 1 adds the decisions record and S111's results after its cross-examination; job 4 adds the decisions record and plain file 111 (for style). **No sandbox holds Avida's source or binary, or any raw output** (traces, ablation lists, saved program populations): those stay in the scratch space, and the build refuses any source outside `Semantics/`. There is no program in any sandbox (no `model/` folder), so the guard refuses every command: GLM may Read, Glob and Grep, and writes nothing. Each brief quotes the owner's words (S20, S21, S23, S28, S43, S56, S60, S61) and asks for objections, each with **the exact fix**, terse, at most about 3,000 words, last line `END OF REPORT`. The briefs, manifests and job list are named, with their md5s, in `tools/s112x_jobs - S112, GLM cross-examination.json`, written by the build and committed before the launch.

- **The call**: glm-5.3 through Claude Code (S29), `--effort medium` (S17), the 1,000,000-token window, 6 attempts, at most 3 answers without END OF REPORT, 7,200 seconds per attempt, `--rule` (this file, committed and unchanged from HEAD), `--brief-md5`, `--manifest-md5`. Up to 3 passes per job. Sandboxes in `<scratchpad>/s112x_sandboxes/`, homes in `<scratchpad>/s112x_homes/`. Returns in `results/S112 What the evolved sums are - GLM cross-examination returns/`.
- **Before the launch**: a dry test of the four sandboxes with a dummy key (built by the helper's own `build_sandbox`; the guard handed a write, `touch`, two `python3 -c`, `cat`, `env`, a redirect and a run of one of the S112 scripts, each to be refused; every sandbox to come back unchanged; no Avida binary, no `.spop`, `.dat`, `.trace` or `.jsonl` file, no file larger than 400,000 bytes), recorded and committed; no other GLM run of this project going, so that no more than four GLM calls run at once.

## How the replies will be read

1. **Nothing is opened until all four calls end.** No reply, receipt, reasoning file, attempt file, stream file or guard log of this cross-examination is opened until every job has ended its last allowed pass: the run log holds `s112x_glm_loop: every pass ended; …` and `loop ended <UTC time>`, and the process in the pid file has exited. The progress lines may be watched; they hold no reply text. If a call is still running 24 hours after the launch, the runner may be stopped by its PID and the calls not ended recorded as not returned.
2. **What counts as a reply**: only `<tag>.response.txt` (or `<tag>_pass<k>.response.txt`); failed calls count neither way; connection failures are not answers; a key in the output or a sandbox not unchanged is reported before anything else is read.
3. **One Opus agent reads every objection and settles each**, by argument from the plan, the results, the scripts, the configuration and Avida's source, or **by rerunning** (Avida in analysis mode, the scripts, or a new check) in the scratch space (`/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-ThreadSmith/8d9323da-c0ec-57ec-91fd-8f99ca99320a/scratchpad`), never in the repository; and records for each: the objection, its settlement (stands, stands in part, does not stand), the reason (or the rerun and its numbers), and what it changes. An objection is a claim until settled; an objection repeated by several jobs decides nothing (arguments, not numbers); silence is not agreement. The agent writes `results/S112 What the evolved sums are - the GLM cross-examination, settled.md`, created at once and filled as it goes.
4. **Findings that stand amend the S112 files in corrected copies**: `… , after the cross-examination.md` (and `.json`) beside the results file, and corrected copies of any script that changes (with its own plain name and note); the files as sent are kept as they were. The plain-words file 112 is updated to match, and its note says it now follows the check. Nothing in the theory's text, formal core, claims or program, any Part A, Part B, S110 or S111 file, the decisions record, the S61 terms file or `authority/` is written.
5. **The owner's words bind every finding as content** (S20 to S61). An objection that would settle for the owner something the S112 files leave open (whether what was found is knowledge; how the owner's question should be read beyond what S60 says) is recorded, not applied (S28, S21). No finding ranks anything (S20).
6. **Records** follow the settlement, by the same agent: an addition to log S112 in the project story and the plain story, and Status, INDEX and README as earlier entries did. Then the owner chooses the next step.

## How the run is launched

From the repository root, after this file's commit is pushed and the build and dry test are committed, one process, detached so that it outlives the agent that starts it, with the key loaded only into its own environment from the session's key file and never opened or printed by the agent, and the other keys unset:

```
setsid nohup bash -c 'cd /home/user/ThreadSmith || exit 1; echo "launched $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"; R="Semantics/results/S112 What the evolved sums are - how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending.md"; { git ls-files --error-unmatch -- "$R" >/dev/null && git diff --quiet HEAD -- "$R"; } || { echo "the reading rule is not committed or differs from HEAD; nothing sent"; exit 1; }; set -a; . <key file>; set +a; unset ATRIA_API_KEY MIMO_API_KEY OPENAI_API_KEY; python3 -B Semantics/tools/s112x_glm_loop.py "Semantics/tools/s112x_jobs - S112, GLM cross-examination.json"; echo "loop ended $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"' > <scratchpad>/s112x_glm_run.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &
```

The process id of the session leader goes in `<scratchpad>/s112x_glm_run.pid`. The launching agent writes `results/S112 What the evolved sums are - GLM cross-examination, launch record.md`, commits it, and hands back once the log shows all four calls sent.

## Unsure

- GLM cannot run Avida or see the traces or the ablation lists; it judges the numbers by their consistency with the scripts, the configuration, the worked examples and each other. A claim it cannot check is to be listed as not reached, not as an objection.
- GLM sees Avida's rules only as S111's build notes and the S112 scripts' citations give them; a rule misread there could pass unnoticed.
- One GLM job per angle may miss what the work also missed.

11	**What had to be removed.** In almost every Avida program (98 in 100), taking out **one single instruction** was enough to stop a given sum while the program went on copying itself. In the other 2 in 100, a second copy of the sum inside the same program meant two instructions had to go together.
12	
13	**What it is.** When those instructions run, they make up a **small fixed wiring diagram**, called here a **circuit**: the numbers handed in go through a few steps of one basic operation (and sometimes an addition or subtraction that behaves the same way), and the result is handed out. 14	
15	The rest of this page explains each of these, with examples.
16	
17	## 2. The words used, with an example
18	
19	**Avida** is a research program that runs a simulated computer. 20	
21	A **sum** here is one of Avida's nine small logic tasks: the simulated computer hands a program numbers, and the program earns a reward if it hands back certain combinations of them. The simplest, NOT, is a number that has a 1 wherever the number handed in has a 0, and a 0 wherever it has a 1. The hardest, EQU, marks, place by place, where two numbers agree. The nine are NOT, NAND, AND, ORN, OR, ANDN, NOR, XOR, EQU.
22	
23	The simulated computer has three **storage places** (Avida calls them registers) and two piles of numbers (stacks). An instruction such as "combine" acts on the storage places; a small **marker** instruction placed right after it can say which storage place it uses.
24	
25	Avida has **one instruction that combines numbers**: it is called `nand`, and it gives, place by place, a 1 unless both numbers have a 1 there. Every one of the nine sums can be built out of it, the way every electronic circuit in a computer can be built out of one kind of switch. Avida also has instructions that add, subtract, add one and take one away.
26	
27	Avida hands a program **three fixed numbers** when it tests it alone. They are handed out **in turn**: the first "read a number" instruction gets the first number, the next gets the second, then the third, then the first again.
28	
29	To **remove** an instruction here means to put in its place an instruction that does nothing (researchers call this instruction ablation; you listed it). A program **stops a sum** if, after the removal, it still copies itself but no longer does the sum.
30	
31	## 3. What had to be removed
32	
33	**An example first.** The most common program doing NOT in one of the nine runs has 110 instructions and is carried by 44 Avida programs in its population. 36	
37	**Now across all the programs.** This was done for every distinct instruction sequence alive at the end of the nine runs: 23,332 of them, carried by 32,193 Avida programs; every single instruction of each removed in turn (2.3 million runs of Avida), and every pair of instructions in every program that copies itself and does a sum (52 million runs).
38	
39	- For **98 in 100** program-and-sum pairs, one instruction was enough. The number of such instructions per program: about 5 for NOT and NAND, 7 for ORN, 10 for ANDN, 13 for AND and OR, 16 for NOR, 22 for EQU, 27 for XOR.
40	- They are the same few kinds everywhere: the read-and-hand-out instruction (a quarter to two fifths of them), `nand` (about a fifth), the markers (about a fifth to a quarter), and the move instructions; for some sums also add, subtract, add one, take one away.

43	- **89 program-and-sum pairs** (NOT and ORN only, 95 Avida programs, in two runs) could not be stopped this way at all: every instruction of their sum is also one of the instructions they need to copy themselves, so removing any of them stops the copying too.
44	
45	So the direct answer to "what needed to be removed": for each program and each sum, **one of a small, listed set of instructions**, and those sets, across thousands of programs, are made of the same kinds of instruction doing the same jobs.
46	
47	## 4. What it is
48	
49	**An example first: EQU**, in the most common EQU program of one run (108 instructions, 28 Avida programs). With the three numbers called A, B and C, Avida's step-by-step record shows these steps, in order:
50	
51	1. combine B and A with `nand`: "not both A and B"; put it on a pile;
52	2. read C and A, and with one `nand`, one addition, one "add one" and one subtraction, turn them into **not A** (C goes in and cancels out);

61	- **A few circuits cover most programs.** NOT: one `nand` of a number with itself, 63 in 100 of the NOT programs. NAND: one `nand` of two numbers, 82 in 100. ORN: two `nand` steps, 69 in 100. 63	- **Some circuits use addition and subtraction** where you might expect only `nand`. These are exact: for example "not both A and C, plus A, plus one" is always "A and not C", for any numbers. 70

79

81	
82	**Tested:** every single removal in every program; every pair in every program that copies itself and does a sum; every three together in the nine most common programs; Avida's step-by-step record of every program, followed with no difference; each circuit's answer checked against Avida's own check, on the three fixed numbers, on all eight combinations of digits, and on 200 other sets of numbers; four kinds of change to Avida.

88	**Unsure:** "the same circuit" counts two circuits as different if they reach the same answer through different additions and subtractions; the job of an instruction that is off the path (for instance an extra read) was read from Avida's record, and checked by removal only in three cases; one step-by-step record per program, on one set of numbers.

91	
92	After GLM's check has been read and this page corrected, the next step I propose: take one program and cut it down, removal by removal, to the **smallest instruction sequence that still copies itself and still does one sum** (you listed this as a minimal instruction sequence), so that you can see the whole thing, copying part and circuit, in one short list. - **Change what `nand` means.** Make the letter for `nand` mean `nor` instead (a 1 only where both numbers have a 0): 98 in 100 programs still copy themselves, but what sums they do changes: of the NAND programs, 97 in 100 now do NOR instead; only 2 in 100 of the OR programs still do OR. What each program then does was said beforehand from its own circuit, and that was right for 99 in 100. Make it mean `and`: almost all sums vanish except AND (73 in 100 remain) and some NOT and ANDN.
- **Remove the input and output channel.** Make the read-and-hand-out letter do nothing: **no program does any sum**, though 83 to 89 in 100 still copy themselves.
- **Hand in other numbers.** Numbers of the kind Avida hands out in its runs: 99 to 100 in 100 still do each sum. Completely random numbers: 66 to 90 in 100. Some programs' other instructions compare the numbers handed in and take a different path when they change, and a few circuits give the right answer only for some numbers.
- **Change all the meanings.** Give the 26 letters the 26 meanings in another order: no program copies itself or does anything.

So the circuit is a circuit **only relative to Avida**: to what its letters mean, to its read-and-hand-out channel, and to the numbers it hands in, in turn. The same letters under other meanings are other circuits, or nothing.

## 6. Tested, not tested, unsure

**Tested:** every single removal in every program; every pair in every program that copies itself and does a sum; every three together in the nine most common programs; Avida's step-by-step record of every program, followed with no difference; each circuit's answer checked against Avida's own check, on the three fixed numbers, on all eight combinations of digits, and on 200 other sets of numbers; four kinds of change to Avida.

**Changed from the plan, and said so in the record:** the first way of writing the circuits down grew too large for the computer's memory in programs that reuse their steps many times, so the job was stopped and the circuits written down more compactly; Avida would not accept a reshuffled instruction set with its markers anywhere, so the markers were kept in front; and some programs that split off an inexact copy are still credited with sums by Avida, which the plan had not expected; they are counted separately.

**Not tested:** removing an instruction by cutting it out (which shifts all later positions), rather than putting a do-nothing in its place; all sets of three or more in every program; the programs inside the full program population, with neighbours, rather than alone.

**Unsure:** "the same circuit" counts two circuits as different if they reach the same answer through different additions and subtractions; the job of an instruction that is off the path (for instance an extra read) was read from Avida's record, and checked by removal only in three cases; one step-by-step record per program, on one set of numbers.

## 7. One next step

After GLM's check has been read and this page corrected, the next step I propose: take one program and cut it down, removal by removal, to the **smallest instruction sequence that still copies itself and still does one sum** (you listed this as a minimal instruction sequence), so that you can see the whole thing, copying part and circuit, in one short list. Which way to take it is yours to choose.
